protocol.name: Web Bot Auth
protocol.full_name: HTTP Message Signatures for automated traffic
protocol.maintainer: IETF Web Bot Auth (webbotauth) working group; editors T. Meunier (Cloudflare) and S. Major (Google)
protocol.newer_version_note: Revision -01 was published in October 2026 and was not analysed here.

summary: Web Bot Auth is a way for bots and AI agents to prove, on every web request, which operator's key signed it. It is aimed at automated traffic on the open web (e.g. AI assistants, search indexing, content aggregation and automated testing), where websites today rely on IP address lists and User-Agent strings that are hard to manage or easy to fake. It is an Internet-Draft of the IETF Web Bot Auth working group, at revision -00 (September 2026). It has public implementations but is not yet an RFC.

The agent's operator publishes its public keys in a key directory at an HTTPS URL. The agent names that URL in a Signature-Agent header and signs each request with HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421), covering at least the target host and a validity window. A website, or a CDN in front of it, fetches the key and checks the signature without any prior relationship with the agent, and can then allow, rate-limit or block that operator. The draft deliberately leaves out who the user is, what the agent may do, whether the operator should be trusted, and how to revoke keys.
how_it_works: The agent's operator creates a signing key and publishes the public key in a JSON key directory (JWKS), by default at a well-known URL on its own domain.

For each request, the agent adds a Signature-Agent header naming that directory and signs the request with an HTTP Message Signature covering the target host, with created and expires times, a keyid and the tag web-bot-auth.
The website, or a proxy or CDN in front of it, reads the signature headers and, if it does not already have the key, fetches it from the Signature-Agent URL.
It verifies the signature and checks that the current time is inside the signature's validity window.
It applies its own policy to the identified operator, e.g. allow, rate-limit or block.

rows.short: Bots and agents sign every HTTP request with a published key
rows.answer: An IETF draft where bots and agents sign every HTTP request with a key published at their own URL, so websites can tell who they are without any prior relationship.

claims.text: Every request is signed with the provider's key.
claims.quote: It proposes that every request from bots be signed by a private key owned by its provider.
Require no pre-established relationship between the two.

rows.short: Bots and agents on the open web
rows.answer: General web traffic from bots and agents (e.g. AI assistants, search indexing, content aggregation and automated testing) to ordinary websites. It works only at the HTTP layer, as signed HTTP headers, so websites need no special client setup. Verification can be done by the website itself or by a proxy or CDN in front of it, which can share cached keys across many websites.

claims.quote: Agents are increasingly used in business and user workflows, including AI assistants, search indexing, content aggregation, and automated testing.
This protocol operates solely at the HTTP layer.

claims.text: Verification by the origin or a fronting proxy.
claims.quote: Signature verification can be performed either directly by origins or delegated to a fronting proxy.
Proxy verification offloads processing and enables shared caching across multiple origins.

rows.answer: Agent: the bot or AI agent that signs each request with its operator's key. Origin: the website that receives signed requests and verifies them, directly or through a fronting proxy or CDN. User: whoever starts the action, a person or another system; the protocol does not identify them. The agent's public keys are served from a key directory at an HTTPS URL.

claims.quote: An entity initiating requests through an agent. May be a human operator or another system.
An HTTP server receiving signed requests that implements the HTTP protocol and verifies

rows.answer: Draft. An Internet-Draft adopted by the IETF Web Bot Auth working group (revision -00, September 2026); it is not yet an RFC, and revision -01 followed in October 2026. The draft lists public implementations of both signing and verifying.

rows.short: RFC 9421, JWKS, JWK thumbprint, well-known URIs
rows.answer: HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) for signing requests; JSON Web Key Sets (RFC 7517) for the key directory; JWK thumbprints (RFC 7638) as key IDs; and a well-known URI (RFC 8615) for the default directory location. Client ID Metadata Documents can be used as another way to discover keys.

rows.short: Operator's key directory URL and key
rows.answer: Partly. The agent identifies itself with the HTTPS URL where its operator publishes its keys, sent in the Signature-Agent header. After verification, the website knows a pair: that URL and a key from it. This names the operator's key directory, which all of the operator's agents share, not an individual agent.

rows.answer: An HTTP Message Signature (RFC 9421) on every request. It must cover the target host (@authority or @target-uri) and include created and expires times, a keyid (a thumbprint of the public key) and the tag web-bot-auth. Covering the method and path is only recommended and no nonce is required, so a signature over the host alone can be reused by anyone who sees it, against the same website, until it expires.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a signature on every request that the site can verify (same as TAP).

This document defines no additional nonce requirements.

rows.answer: Recommended, not enforced. Every signature must carry created and expires times, and the draft recommends that expiry be no more than 24 hours, but it sets no rule for verifiers. Because a signature over the host alone can be reused until it expires, a long expiry also widens the window for replay.

rows.answer: Yes. The website (or its proxy) reads the Signature-Agent header, fetches the operator's keys from that URL if it does not already have them, and verifies the signature and its time window. No prior relationship with the agent is needed. Verifiers should cache the key directory and refresh it when it expires, so key changes reach them only after that.

rows.answer: No. The signature proves that the request was signed with a key from the operator's directory, which all of the operator's agents share. The draft states that this says nothing about who operates the agent, whether it is benign, or whether the request is authorized. Human users are not authenticated.

rows.answer: No (out of scope). The draft does not define authorization or delegation, so the website learns nothing about what the agent is allowed to do. What it gets is a reliable operator identity to which it can apply its own policy, e.g. allowlisting, denylisting or rate limits per operator.

rows.answer: No one, by design. A valid signature shows that the key came from the URL in the Signature-Agent header, not that the operator of that URL is honest or is who it appears to be. The draft does not define how trust is built, held or shared between websites, so each website decides for itself.
rows.rating_reason: Red: trust is explicitly out of scope; registries are outside the protocol.

claims.quote: It does not define how trust is accrued, held, or exchanged, and it defines no mechanism for one origin to convey an opinion about an Agent to another.

claims.text: The URL does not vouch for honesty.

rows.answer: None. The draft states that it does not define a revocation mechanism. If a key is compromised, the only remedy is to remove it from the directory, and each verifier stops accepting it when its cached copy expires. Websites can still block an operator's URL or key on their own.
rows.rating_reason: Red: the draft states it defines no revocation.

claims.quote: It is not a revocation mechanism, and this document does not define any.

claims.text: Key removal is the only remedy and waits for caches.
claims.quote: Removing a compromised key from the directory is the only remedy, and it takes effect at each verifier on its next refresh

rows.answer: No by default. The draft defines no contact or escalation channel. A separate individual draft (draft-meunier-webbotauth-registry-03) defines a Signature Agent Card whose optional contacts field lists ways to reach the operator, typically email addresses.

goals_reading.access_control: The website learns only which operator's key signed the request. It can allow, rate-limit or block that operator, but receives no permissions or scopes.
goals_reading.incident_response: Each website can block an operator's URL or key on its own. There is no revocation, and nothing reaches a specific agent instance.
goals_reading.accountability: An action can be traced to the holder of the operator's key, not to a user or an agent instance.
